name: Engram Alpha
tagline: The graph memory you can see, edit, and measure
description: Local-first reasoning memory for coding assistants that stores decisions, problems, and insights as a typed graph you can see and edit on a canvas embedded in JetBrains and VS Code. Retrieval changes ship only with a measured benchmark run.
approachDetail: Typed knowledge graph — 8 node types (Decision, Principle, Caution, Problem, Resolution, Insight, Intent, Anchor) and 7 sentence-shaped edge types (because, replaces, conflicts-with, ...) — with local bge-small embeddings (fastembed/ONNX). Ontology and retrieval policy are per-graph configurable since v0.7.0; a local encoder-only cortex (cross-encoder reranker + NLI) sharpens ranking and flags contradictions. No LLM runs in the daemon, by design
searchDetail: Hybrid cosine + FTS5 keyword recall (keyword weighted 0.15), re-scored by a local cross-encoder that votes rather than decides, with a trust term; hits carry up to 5 one-hop neighbors, conflicts and supersessions first. Delivery is calibrated: results below a floor are cut, the ranked list is trimmed where its score curve falls off a cliff (adaptive-k), and a self-calibrated confidence line labels answers 'likely not in memory' without cutting them. Separate bounded graph-traversal and check_claim tools
storageDetail: One git-ignored .engram/graph.tepin per repository. TepinDB is a small embedded database for CLI tools, written alongside Engram Alpha by the same author, and the default for new graphs since v0.6.2; a SQLite + sqlite-vec driver remains behind the same Store trait so existing graph.db files keep working, and migration is automatic
mcpDetail: rmcp server over stdio and streamable HTTP, exposing brief, search, traverse, check_claim, add_note(s), link/unlink, update_node(s)/update_edge, approve_node, list_suspects/resolve_suspect, list_open, list_drift, list_nodes, list_projects, get_node, timeline, audit, describe_ontology and set_version. Deliberately no delete, pin or register tools — those are user-only gestures in the pane
toolSupportDetail: Ships a Claude Code plugin and skill (three capture-aggressiveness variants, generated per graph from its ontology), a JetBrains plugin (JCEF tool window) and a VS Code extension (secondary-sidebar webview) embedding the same graph pane
scopesDetail: A graph per repository plus a user-level home graph; a machine-wide registry federates them, so reads can span every registered project with provenance on foreign hits and a locality prior that keeps the local canon ranked first. Writes stay scoped to one graph — fanning a write across projects is refused
duplicateDetail: Write-time same-type cosine pre-check at 0.90: add_note returns {matched, created: false} instead of creating a near-duplicate. A local NLI cross-encoder screens look-alike pairs and queues suspects for human judgment (conflict / replaces / dismiss) — the model nominates, the person decides; writes landing near contradicted or superseded knowledge return warnings. replaces-edges retire predecessors along any edge path
retentionDetail: Trust (0..1) is computed at read time and reads only deliberate acts — retrieval never refreshes it, because being findable proves nothing. Stable knowledge holds trust flat until a judged conflict demotes it (withdrawing the conflict withdraws the demotion); episodic and volatile knowledge decays with time. A decay pass archives unapproved episodic/volatile nodes 14 days after going stale, and replaces-edges auto-archive superseded nodes. Pinning and hard delete are user-only
multiUserDetail: Single-user, per-repo database; team sharing and repo sync are permanently out of scope for this product
crossMachineDetail: The graph is a git-ignored local file; the registry federates projects on one machine only. Manual JSON export, no sync
webUiDetail: Vue graph canvas served by the local daemon and embedded in the IDE panes: node and edge editing, four layouts, a timeline/feed view with lenses synced to the graph, a conflict-judgment worklist, graph-health and checkup strips, a redactor for excluding content, per-graph ontology and policy settings, and a Memory Lens showing exactly what the assistant receives
tokenBudgetingDetail: The session-start brief takes a character budget (default ~16k chars, about 4k tokens) and caps its sections; search takes a result limit, caps neighbors at 5 per hit, and offers compact/snippet/full detail levels so depth is paid for on demand. Delivery then trims adaptively at the score curve's knee rather than a fixed depth — measured at 315 tokens per query against 2,673 for pure-vector RAG at the same recall (1,500 notes, 4,500 questions)
contextInjectionDetail: Retrieval is automatic, capture is cooperative. Shipped hooks inject the session brief at session start and surface memory attached to files as they are read or edited; beyond that the assistant calls MCP tools guided by the shipped skill (search before non-trivial work, silent batched writes at stopping points), so nothing is captured ambiently
networkDetail: Fully local — no remote services or API keys, and no LLM in the daemon. The embedding, reranker and NLI models are ONNX and downloaded once to a machine-wide cache on first run; models are selectable and hot-swappable
auditTrailDetail: Every node and edge mutation appends a journal row with before/after JSON, action, origin, session id, working directory, pid and the product version, queryable from the pane and the audit MCP tool. Nodes additionally carry provenance and supersession chains that keep archived predecessors
pros: Retrieval is measured, not asserted: an offline harness (4,500 questions over 1,500 notes, plus never-written subjects) reports what retrieval costs as well as what it finds, and the receipts are committed in the repo
Delivers ~315 tokens per query against ~2,673 for pure-vector RAG at the same recall, because delivery is trimmed at the score curve's knee instead of a fixed depth

Says when it does not know: a self-calibrated confidence line (no labels, no LLM) labels answers 'likely not in memory', taking the false-positive rate on never-written subjects from 1.00 to 0.02 without cutting a single result
The memory is visible and editable — a graph canvas embedded in JetBrains / VS Code, not a hidden store
Active conflict surfacing: a local NLI model screens look-alike pairs and queues them for human judgment (conflict / replaces / dismiss), measured in its own harness
Typed, sentence-shaped ontology (a Decision links `because` a Principle), configurable per graph, instead of freeform text blobs
Fully local single Rust binary with a full before/after audit journal; no keys, no services, no LLM in the daemon
cons: Single-user, single-machine — team sharing and repo sync are permanently out of scope, not merely unbuilt (manual JSON export only)
Capture is cooperative: it depends on the assistant following the shipped skill, and nothing is captured ambiently
The 'likely not in memory' hedge leads roughly 45% of the lowest-confidence answerable replies — deliberately cautious, and tunable per graph, but it will read as hedging
One daemon per repository to run, and onboarding still involves several manual steps
Encoder-only by design: no LLM summarization, consolidation or synthesis of memories
Benchmarks are self-run on a synthetic invented-subject corpus — reproducible by one command, but not third-party verified
notes: "Alpha" is part of the product name, not a version tag — several unrelated projects are also named "engram", including the Python entry in this comparison. The JetBrains plugin is Kotlin/JCEF; the pane is Vue 3 + Vue Flow. Benchmark figures cite eval/README.md in the repository, which documents the harness and the refuted alternatives alongside the shipped results.
